warmup.q: A Kotlin class is marked @OpenForProxies, but the build applies no compiler plugins. What does javap show for the class?
options: public final class: an annotation is only a label until a plugin reads it
It depends on the JDK version
The class doesn't compile until you add open
warmup.why: Kotlin makes classes and their members final by default, and an annotation is just data: it changes nothing unless a compiler plugin reads it. That's what the all-open plugin does, as the first section shows. Many people pick the first option, because the name sounds like an instruction and because Java classes are open by default.

opening:
Picture the print shop's print line, where a job goes in as a file and comes out as paper. On the way, machines change every job that passes. One takes off the shrink-wrap so that a cover sheet can go in front, one adds a blank form at the back, one clips on a slip that describes the job. Each acts on a note on the job's ticket.

The Kotlin compiler has a line like that, and compiler plugins are its machines. You mark a class with an annotation, a label that tools can read. A plugin then changes what the compiler writes for it: it takes away a final, adds a constructor, or writes a whole new class. The trap is that your source shows none of it: the class you read is not the class the JVM loads.

In the last lesson, contracts told the compiler facts; now plugins change what it writes. We'll open classes for frameworks that subclass them, add an empty constructor for frameworks that fill objects in later, write JSON with a serializer nobody typed, and meet tools that write source files instead. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started on the shop's print line, where machines change every job as it passes. Compiler plugins are those machines: all-open takes the final off for frameworks that subclass, no-arg adds a blank constructor for frameworks that fill objects in later, and kotlinx.serialization clips a serializer to each class. That ends the track: every feature in it was code the compiler writes.

In your own build, run javap on one class a plugin should have changed, and check that it did.

Next, in this part's capstone, we'll build one small library with these tools, starting with a sealed event model. How do you make the compiler list every place that must change when a new kind of event appears?

sections.h: Kotlin classes are final, and frameworks that subclass them need them open
sections.html:
Many libraries add behavior to your classes without touching your source. A framework is a library that calls your code, rather than the other way round. Many frameworks do it with a proxy: a class they generate that extends yours and overrides each method. The override does some work before and after calling your original through super. A timing proxy starts a clock, calls your method, and writes down how long it took. Write such a subclass by hand for the shop's PrintQueue, and the problem shows at once:

Java
class LoggedPrintQueue extends PrintQueue {      // error: cannot inherit from final PrintQueue
    @Override public String print(String job) { return super.print(job); }
}
Kotlin
class TimedPrintQueue : PrintQueue() {             // error: this type is final, so it cannot be extended.
    override fun print(job: String): String =      // error: 'print' in 'PrintQueue' is final
        super.print(job)                           //        and cannot be overridden.
}

Kotlin classes and their members are final unless you write open: nobody may extend them or override their methods. That default is a good one, because a class then behaves exactly as its author wrote it. But a framework that generates subclasses hits the same wall as your hand-written one, only later, while the program starts. You could write open on every class and every method a framework touches, and nobody keeps that up for long.

On the print line, a final class is a job that arrives shrink-wrapped and ready to ship. Nobody can slip a cover sheet in front of it.

A compiler plugin is a jar (the zip file a Java library ships in) that the Kotlin compiler loads to change what it writes into class files. The all-open plugin "makes classes and their members open at compile time without requiring the open keyword". It does that for every class that carries an annotation you name in the build, or whose superclass does. It's the machine that takes the shrink-wrap off every job with the right note on its ticket. This lab module names workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies for all-open, and a second marker for the plugin of the next section:

// labs/kotlin/build.gradle.kts (the version, 2.4.21, is set once in the root build file)
plugins {
    kotlin("plugin.allopen")
    kotlin("plugin.noarg")
    kotlin("plugin.serialization")
}

allOpen { annotation("workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies") }
noArg { annotation("workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity") }

javap on the demo's PrintQueue then shows public class and public java.lang.String print(java.lang.String), with no final in sight. What the plugin leaves alone matters just as much. Private members stay private, the field behind traySize stays private final, and the unmarked PlainHelper stays public final class. The plugin matches the annotation by its full name, package included, so an annotation with the same simple name in another package does nothing at all.

An annotation is only a note on the ticket. A plugin named in the build is what acts on it.

The figure puts the three plugins of this lesson side by side. Each one reads an annotation while the code compiles, and each one changes the class file in its own way: it removes a modifier, adds a constructor, or adds a whole class. The second machine is for frameworks with a different need.

try.title: Open a class without writing open
steps: Run AllOpenDemo, then AllOpenDemoJava, which extends the same Kotlin class from Java.
Run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/demo workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.PrintQueue from labs/. Which members are still final?
Delete @OpenForProxies above PrintQueue. Predict the errors, run, and put it back.

code.title: AllOpenDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies import java.lang.reflect.Modifier /** Marked for all-open: the plugin makes the class and its members open at compile time. */ @OpenForProxies class PrintQueue { val traySize: Int = 500 fun print(job: String): String = "printed $job from a tray of $traySize sheets" private fun secret(): Int = 42 // private stays private, and final } /** Not marked: final, like every Kotlin class by default. */ class PlainHelper { fun help(): String = "help" } /** What a framework generates at build or run time: a subclass that wraps every call. */ class TimedPrintQueue : PrintQueue() { override fun print(job: String): String { val start = System.nanoTime() try { return super.print(job) } finally { println(" print took ${(System.nanoTime() - start) / 1_000} us") } } } fun describe(cls: Class<*>) { val methods = cls.declaredMethods.sortedBy { it.name }.joinToString { m -> val kind = when { Modifier.isPrivate(m.modifiers) -> "private" Modifier.isFinal(m.modifiers) -> "final" else -> "open" } "${m.name}:$kind" } println("${cls.simpleName}: ${if (Modifier.isFinal(cls.modifiers)) "final" else "open"} class; $methods") } fun main() { describe(PrintQueue::class.java) describe(PlainHelper::class.java) val queue: PrintQueue = TimedPrintQueue() println(queue.print("flyer.pdf")) // Wrong move. Delete @OpenForProxies above PrintQueue, predict, run. }

Java classes are open unless you write final, so Java can extend the * Kotlin class only because all-open removed its final. Remove the marker and javac says: * "cannot inherit from final PrintQueue". */ public class AllOpenDemoJava { static final class LoggedPrintQueue extends PrintQueue { @Override public String print(String job) { System.out.println(" log: printing " + job); return super.print(job); } } public static void main(String[] args) { PrintQueue queue = new LoggedPrintQueue(); System.out.println(queue.print("flyer.pdf")); AllOpenDemoKt.describe(PlainHelper.class); } }

Ignore the timing: one cold call measures class loading, not the proxy. javap shows public class PrintQueue, private final int traySize and private int secret(): only the field keeps its final. Without the marker, the build fails with this type is final, so it cannot be extended. and 'print' in 'PrintQueue' is final and cannot be overridden., and the Java twin would get cannot inherit from final PrintQueue.

aside.title: Which annotations does my framework need?
aside.html: Real frameworks come with presets, ready-made lists of annotations. kotlin-spring is all-open with the annotations of Spring, a widely used Java framework for web services, already listed: @Component, @Transactional and a few more. Presets can lag behind their framework, though. In the Kotlin 2.4.21 plugin, the quarkus preset still lists only the old javax.enterprise.context annotations. Quarkus 3, another framework for services, uses jakarta.enterprise.context, so a class marked with the new name stays final. Whatever your framework, name the annotations it needs yourself in allOpen { annotation(...) }, and check one class with javap after every change to the build.

video.title: A proxy must subclass your class, and Kotlin classes are final; a compiler plugin changes what kotlinc emits: all-open drops final, no-arg adds a hidden empty constructor, serialization writes a serializer class

sections.h: no-arg: an empty constructor for frameworks that build objects first, minus your initializers
sections.html:
Some libraries build your objects in two steps. A library that loads records from a database, for example, first calls a constructor with no parameters to get an empty object. Then it sets each field from the stored record. So it needs every such class to have a constructor with no parameters that isn't private. The shop's JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) has none. By hand, you'd add one:

Java
public class JobRow {
    private String id;
    private int pages;
    private String status = "NEW";

    protected JobRow() { }                          // for the database library
    public JobRow(String id, int pages) { this.id = id; this.pages = pages; }
}
Kotlin
class JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) {
    var status: String = "NEW"

    constructor() : this("", 0)                    // the hand-written version: invented values
}

The hand-written Kotlin constructor works, but it invents an empty id and zero pages, and now any Kotlin caller can create that half-made row by mistake. The no-arg plugin generates the constructor instead, for classes with an annotation you configure, here workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity. The docs say it's "annotated with @Deprecated at the HIDDEN level, so you can call it from Java but not from Kotlin". javap -v shows both annotations on it, kotlin.Deprecated with level=HIDDEN and java.lang.Deprecated. The demo shows the two sides: Kotlin's JobRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'., and Java's new JobRow() compiles, with only a deprecation note from javac.

On the print line, no-arg is the machine that adds a blank form at the back of every job marked for it, so that a clerk further down can fill it in.

Now the trap, and the picture shows it. The blank form is really blank. The generated constructor runs no property initializers: its bytecode is three instructions, aload_0, invokespecial Object.<init> and return, and nothing else. The option that would run them, invokeInitializers, is "disabled by default". So after new JobRow(), status holds null, even though Kotlin declared it a non-null String with the value "NEW". The first status.length in Kotlin code throws a NullPointerException. A paper form would at least have "status: NEW" printed on it.

For a database library that's usually fine, because it sets every stored field right afterwards. For anything else, turn invokeInitializers on, or don't rely on initializers in those classes.

A no-arg constructor skips your initializers. Don't trust a field of an object you didn't build yourself.

Hibernate is the best-known such library for Java, and it follows JPA, the Java standard for mapping classes to database tables. For Hibernate and other JPA libraries, use kotlin-jpa rather than configuring no-arg yourself. It is no-arg with a preset for @Entity, @Embeddable and @MappedSuperclass, in both the javax.persistence and jakarta.persistence packages. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, the Gradle org.jetbrains.kotlin.plugin.jpa plugin also applies all-open with a JPA preset, so that, in the release notes' words, "lazy associations work as expected instead of causing eager loading". On older Kotlin versions you had to add all-open for those classes yourself.

The first two machines change the shape of a class. The third writes code the class never had.

try.title: Build an object the way a database library does
steps: Run NoArgDemo, then NoArgDemoJava. Predict blank.status before you look.
Uncomment the wrong move in NoArgDemo.kt, predict, run, and comment it out again.
In NoArgDemo.kt, add println(blank.status.length) at the end of main. Predict what happens, then run.

code.title: NoArgDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity /** no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor that only Java and reflection can call. */ @NoArgEntity class JobRow(val id: String, var pages: Int) { var status: String = "NEW" } fun main() { // the way a database library builds an empty object before it fills in the columns val blank = JobRow::class.java.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() println("blank.pages = ${blank.pages}") println("blank.status is null: ${(blank.status as String?) == null}") // declared String, holds null println("normal status = ${JobRow("job-1", 12).status}") // Wrong move. Uncomment, predict, run. // val direct = JobRow() }

alt.title: NoArgDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; /** * Java twin of NoArgDemo.kt. Java can call the generated constructor directly: it is hidden from * Kotlin with @Deprecated(level = HIDDEN), which javac doesn't enforce. */ public class NoArgDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { JobRow blank = new JobRow(); // compiles in Java System.out.println("blank.pages = " + blank.getPages()); System.out.println("blank.status = " + blank.getStatus()); // null: the initializer never ran System.out.println("blank.getId() = " + blank.getId()); } }

try.expect: Both show pages = 0 and a null status, and the Java twin also prints getId() = null: the generated constructor sets nothing and runs no initializer. The Kotlin call JobRow() fails with no value passed for parameter 'id'. and the same for pages. The added line compiles, because status is declared String, and throws NullPointerException: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because the return value of "...JobRow.getStatus()" is null.

sections.h: kotlinx.serialization writes the serializer while your code compiles
sections.html:
The shop's app records what happens to each job as events: a job was queued, printed, jammed or cancelled. To save those events in a file, or send them to another program, the app turns each one into text and back. The usual format for that text is JSON, {"jobId":"job-1","pages":12}: names and values in braces, readable by people and by almost every programming language.

Most JSON libraries on the JVM work by reflection, which means inspecting a class while the program runs: they find its constructor and its properties, and guess how to fill them. Kotlin classes make the guessing harder, with default arguments and non-null types that the JVM knows nothing about. kotlinx.serialization doesn't guess. "When you annotate a class with @Serializable, the Kotlin serialization plugin generates a KSerializer for that class."

The demo's Queued gets a nested class, Queued$$serializer, that implements GeneratedSerializer<Queued> with real serialize and deserialize methods, plus Queued.serializer() on the companion object. On the print line, it's the machine that clips a slip to each job, listing its fields one by one. With the slip, anyone further down can write the job out as text and read it back. Without the plugin, Queued.serializer() is unresolved reference 'serializer'.

Java
// Java's usual approach, with Jackson, a JSON library that reads these annotations by reflection
@JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type")
@JsonSubTypes({
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Queued.class, name = "queued"),
    @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = Cancelled.class, name = "cancelled")
})
public sealed interface JobEvent permits Queued, Cancelled { String jobId(); }

String json = new ObjectMapper().writeValueAsString(events);
Kotlin
@Serializable
sealed interface JobEvent { val jobId: String }

@Serializable @SerialName("queued")
data class Queued(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val paper: String = "A4") : JobEvent

@Serializable @SerialName("cancelled")
data class Cancelled(override val jobId: String, val reason: String? = null) : JobEvent

private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false }
val text = lenient.encodeToString(events)      // events: List<JobEvent>

A sealed hierarchy, a base type whose subclasses are all known when the code compiles, is what the docs call "closed polymorphism". The plugin knows every subclass, so it can write and read a "type" field with no registration. That field is the class discriminator: it tells the reader which subclass an object is. Three details decide what the JSON looks like.

The discriminator is written only when the static type, the type the compiler sees, is the base. List<JobEvent> gets "type":"queued", while Json.encodeToString(q) with q typed Queued gets none. Its value is the fully qualified class name unless you set @SerialName, so without it, moving a class to another package changes your saved files. And the default Json leaves out properties that equal their default (encodeDefaults is off), writes nulls, and rejects keys it doesn't know: Encountered an unknown key 'tray'.

For saved events, that last default matters most. A newer version of the app adds a tray field, and every older reader with the default Json puts the whole file down at the first key it doesn't know. So set ignoreUnknownKeys = true. Build one Json instance and reuse it: the docs say instances "are immutable and thread-safe", and reusing one is faster. The JSON format is Stable; HOCON, ProtoBuf, CBOR and Properties are still Experimental.

Pin every subtype with @SerialName, and tolerate unknown keys in data that outlives one version of the app.

The generated serializer is plain bytecode, with no reflection while the program runs. Java can call it too, as the demo's twin does with Queued.Companion.serializer().

All three machines so far change the compiler's own output. A second family of tools leaves the class files alone and writes new source files instead.

try.title: Read the JSON a sealed hierarchy produces
steps: Run SerializationDemo. Before you do, predict which lines will contain "type".
Remove @SerialName("queued") from Queued and run again. What is the type value now?
Run SerializationDemoJava, which uses the generated serializer from Java through Queued.Companion.serializer().

code.title: SerializationDemo.kt
code.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo import kotlinx.serialization.SerialName import kotlinx.serialization.SerializationException import kotlinx.serialization.Serializable import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json @Serializable sealed interface JobEvent { val jobId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("queued") data class Queued(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val paper: String = "A4") : JobEvent @Serializable @SerialName("cancelled") data class Cancelled(override val jobId: String, val reason: String? = null) : JobEvent private val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } fun main() { val events: List<JobEvent> = listOf(Queued("job-1", 12), Cancelled("job-1")) val text = lenient.encodeToString(events) println(text) println("round trip equal: ${lenient.decodeFromString<List<JobEvent>>(text) == events}") val q = Queued("job-2", 1) println("static type Queued: ${Json.encodeToString(q)}") println("static type JobEvent: ${Json.encodeToString<JobEvent>(q)}") val newer = """{"type":"queued","jobId":"job-3","pages":5,"tray":"2"}""" println("lenient: ${lenient.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(newer)}") try { Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(newer) } catch (e: SerializationException) { println("default Json: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}") } println("generated serializer: ${Queued.serializer().javaClass.name}") }

alt.title: SerializationDemoJava.java
alt.html: package workbench.kotlin.l06.demo; import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json; /** * Java twin of SerializationDemo.kt. The plugin's output is ordinary bytecode, so Java can use it: * Queued.Companion.serializer() returns the generated KSerializer, and Json.Default does the rest. * Java code normally uses a reflection-based JSON library instead; this shows what the plugin generated. */ public class SerializationDemoJava { public static void main(String[] args) { Queued q = new Queued("job-2", 1, "A4"); String text = Json.Default.encodeToString(Queued.Companion.serializer(), q); System.out.println("Java, static type Queued: " + text); Queued back = Json.Default.decodeFromString(Queued.Companion.serializer(), text); System.out.println("decoded: " + back + ", equal: " + back.equals(q)); System.out.println("generated serializer: " + Queued.Companion.serializer().getClass().getName()); } }

try.expect: The list prints [{"type":"queued","jobId":"job-1","pages":12},{"type":"cancelled","jobId":"job-1"}]: no paper (it equals its default) and no reason (null, with explicitNulls = false). The static-type Queued line has no type; the JobEvent line has one. The lenient instance ignores tray, and the default one fails with Encountered an unknown key 'tray'. Without @SerialName the type becomes workbench.kotlin.l06.demo.Queued. The Java twin prints the JSON of one Queued and the class name Queued$$serializer.

sections.h: KSP and kapt write new source files instead
sections.html:
The three plugins above change the compiler's output from the inside. A second family of tools generates new source files from your annotations, the way Java's annotation processors do. An annotation processor is a program that runs during compilation, reads the annotations in your code and writes extra source files, which are then compiled with the rest. Libraries use them for code that would be dull to write by hand: mappers that copy fields from one class to another, or the glue that builds your objects and hands each one the helpers it needs.

kapt runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code. The docs say it "generates stub files from Kotlin source code and then runs the Java annotation processors on those stubs". Those stubs are Java declarations of your Kotlin classes, written only so that a Java processor can read them. The migration guide calls them "expensive": they "significantly increase build time" and lose Kotlin-specific features.

KSP, Kotlin Symbol Processing, is the Kotlin-native alternative, "a source code generation framework for Kotlin". Its processors read Kotlin declarations directly, and its README says they "can run up to 2x faster" than kapt. The limits are part of the design: KSP processors "can't examine expressions or statements, and they can't modify the source code". They only add new files.

On the print line, kapt and KSP aren't machines at all. They are a second shop that prints extra pages from the notes on your tickets, and the extra pages then join the job. kapt first copies every page into another language so that its workers can read it. KSP reads the original.

Two version facts matter today. KSP2 "is no longer a compiler plugin" and is built on the same compiler APIs as IntelliJ IDEA. And since KSP 2.3.0, KSP1 is deprecated and "KSP version is no longer tied to the Kotlin compiler version", so a KSP release number no longer has to match your Kotlin version.

My rule: use KSP whenever the library ships a KSP processor, and kapt only for processors that exist just for Java. Watch the build time when you add kapt: every module that uses it pays for the stub step on each build.

That's also the limit of this whole family of tools, plugins included. They change what the compiler writes, and your source doesn't show it. A class that reads as final is open, a constructor nobody wrote exists, and a serializer nobody typed runs. When something surprises you, javap shows what is really there, and the build file says who put it there.

A check to end on, and the answer follows from how the serialization plugin works: a module depends on the kotlinx-serialization-json library but doesn't apply kotlin("plugin.serialization"). You mark a class @Serializable and call Queued.serializer(). What happens, and at which stage? (It fails at compile time with unresolved reference 'serializer'.: the annotation compiles because it lives in the library, but nobody generates the companion function.)

compare.title: A proxy-ready service and a database row: Java as written vs Kotlin with plugins

java.title: Beans.java
java.html: public class SheetPlanner { // open by default in Java public int sheetsFor(int pages) { return (pages + 1) / 2; } } public class JobRecord { // open by default private String id; private int pages; private String status = "NEW"; // runs in every constructor protected JobRecord() { } // the no-arg constructor, written by hand public JobRecord(String id, int pages) { this.id = id; this.pages = pages; } }

kotlin.title: Beans.kt
kotlin.html: @OpenForProxies // all-open is configured for this annotation class SheetPlanner { fun sheetsFor(pages: Int): Int = (pages + 1) / 2 } @NoArgEntity @OpenForProxies // no-arg adds the constructor, all-open the open class JobRecord(val id: String, var pages: Int) { var status: String = "NEW" // skipped by the generated no-arg constructor }

compare.note: Java gets proxy-ready classes for free: classes and methods are open unless marked final, and you write the no-arg constructor yourself, where field initializers run as usual. Kotlin's defaults point the other way, so the plugins put back what frameworks need, at compile time, driven by annotations. The class files end up close to the Java ones, with one difference that bites: Kotlin's generated no-arg constructor skips property initializers unless you enable invokeInitializers, so status is null on a fresh instance, while Java's hand-written constructor runs status = "NEW".

worked.title: Add a field to saved job events without breaking older readers

steps.say: Version 1 of the shop's app saves job events to a file, and a second program, the label printer, reads them with the default Json. Here are both sides, with a Java reader that uses Jackson.
steps.code: // Java reader with Jackson: by default it also fails on unknown properties ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper(); Printed p = mapper.readValue(line, Printed.class);

alt.html: @Serializable @SerialName("printed") data class Printed(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int) : JobEvent val event = Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(line) // the default Json: strict

steps.say: Version 2 adds a tray field, and the app is updated first. The label printer, still on version 1, now fails on every new line, because unknown keys "result in an error" by default.
steps.code: // version 2 writes {"type":"printed","jobId":"job-7","pages":12,"tray":"2"} Json.decodeFromString<JobEvent>(v2) // SerializationException: ... Encountered an unknown key 'tray' at path: $

alt.html: mapper.readValue(v2, Printed.class); // Jackson: UnrecognizedPropertyException, unless FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is turned off

steps.say: Configure the reader once, in one shared instance: tolerate new keys, keep every @SerialName stable, and give new fields defaults so that old lines still decode.
steps.code: // 1. one instance, reused: immutable and thread-safe val events = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } // 2. a new field gets a default, so version 1 lines without it still decode @Serializable @SerialName("printed") data class Printed(override val jobId: String, val pages: Int, val tray: String? = null) : JobEvent

alt.html: ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper() .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);

steps.say: Check the other direction. A version-1 reader that doesn't know a new subtype, say "type":"recycled", still fails, and it should: ignoreUnknownKeys covers fields, not types. When you add a subtype, update the readers before the writers.

lab.title: A serializable event hierarchy and proxy-ready classes
steps: Read Annotations.kt and the two plugin lines in labs/kotlin/build.gradle.kts. The annotations do nothing by themselves; the plugins look for their names.
Run the tests. All seven fail.
In JobEvents.kt, add @Serializable and @SerialName (TODO 1), create the shared Json (TODO 2), and write encodeEvents and decodeEvents (TODOs 3 and 4).
In Beans.kt, mark SheetPlanner with @OpenForProxies (TODO 5), and JobRecord with @NoArgEntity and @OpenForProxies (TODO 6).
Run until all seven pass, including EventsFromJavaTest. Then run javap -p -cp kotlin/build/classes/kotlin/main workbench.kotlin.l06.JobRecord and find the constructor nobody wrote.
hints: encodeToString and decodeFromString are extension functions with reified types: json.encodeToString(events) and json.decodeFromString<List<JobEvent>>(text), or let the return type infer it.
The "type" field appears because the static type is List<JobEvent>, the sealed base. You don't configure it.
Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; explicitNulls = false } covers both rules. Leave encodeDefaults alone: off is the default, and the test expects paper to be left out.
The marker annotations live in package workbench.kotlin: import workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies and workbench.kotlin.NoArgEntity.
lab.done: All seven tests in PluginsTest and EventsFromJavaTest pass.

drill.title: Write a serializable parcel hierarchy from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a sealed ParcelEvent with two subtypes, ParcelWeighed(parcelId, grams) and ParcelSent(parcelId, sentAtEpochMs), serialized with the stable type names parcel_weighed and parcel_sent, and a shared Json that tolerates new fields. Then write the Java version with Jackson annotations. Where does each version find the subtypes?

answer.html: @Serializable sealed interface ParcelEvent { val parcelId: String } @Serializable @SerialName("parcel_weighed") data class ParcelWeighed(override val parcelId: String, val grams: Long) : ParcelEvent @Serializable @SerialName("parcel_sent") data class ParcelSent(override val parcelId: String, val sentAtEpochMs: Long) : ParcelEvent // the plugin finds the subtypes at compile time, from the sealed hierarchy val parcelJson = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }

alt.title: ParcelEvent.java
alt.html: // Jackson finds the subtypes at run time, from these annotations @JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type") @JsonSubTypes({ @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = ParcelWeighed.class, name = "parcel_weighed"), @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = ParcelSent.class, name = "parcel_sent") }) public sealed interface ParcelEvent permits ParcelWeighed, ParcelSent { String parcelId(); } record ParcelWeighed(String parcelId, long grams) implements ParcelEvent {} record ParcelSent(String parcelId, long sentAtEpochMs) implements ParcelEvent {} ObjectMapper mapper = new ObjectMapper() .configure(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, false);

recap: A compiler plugin changes what kotlinc writes into class files, driven by annotations you name in the build. The annotations do nothing on their own.

all-open removes final from marked classes and their members (not private members, not fields), so a framework can subclass them. kotlin-spring and kotlin-jpa are presets; when a preset lags, name the annotations yourself.
no-arg adds a zero-argument constructor, hidden from Kotlin, callable from Java and reflection. It skips property initializers unless invokeInitializers is on.

kotlinx.serialization generates a $$serializer class at compile time. A sealed base gets a "type" discriminator: pin it with @SerialName, reuse one Json, and set ignoreUnknownKeys for data that outlives one version.
KSP and kapt generate new source files. Prefer KSP; kapt runs Java processors on generated stubs and costs build time.
The limit: none of this shows in your source. javap shows what the plugins really wrote, and the build file says which plugin wrote it.

explain.prompt: A teammate's Kotlin class carries the annotation their framework uses, yet the framework's timing proxy never runs, and javap shows public final class. Explain what's going on in the class file and what you'd change.
explain.answer: Kotlin compiles classes and their methods as final unless something opens them. The framework adds its timing through a generated subclass that overrides the class's methods, and a final class or method can't be overridden. The all-open plugin is supposed to remove final from classes with certain annotations, but it only does that for the annotations it's told about, matched by their full names, package included. Here the build either doesn't apply all-open at all, or names a different annotation, for example a preset that still lists an older package name for the framework's annotation. The annotation on the class is only data, so nothing acts on it and the class stays final. I'd list the exact annotation the class uses in allOpen { annotation("...") }, rebuild, and check with javap that final is gone from the class and its public methods.

deeper.html:
The presets inside the 2.4.21 all-open plugin, read from the plugin's own classes, say more than the docs page. spring lists @Component, @Transactional, @Async, @Cacheable, @SpringBootTest and also org.springframework.validation.annotation.Validated, which the docs page leaves out. micronaut lists four of that framework's annotations for adding behavior to methods, jpa lists Entity, Embeddable and MappedSuperclass in both packages, and quarkus lists only the two old javax scopes. When a framework moves its annotations to a new package, presets lag behind, and listing annotations by name is the only setting you control.

On the command line the same plugins take -P options, which helps when you test an idea with plain kotlinc: -Xplugin=<allopen jar> -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.allopen:annotation=workbench.kotlin.OpenForProxies, and for no-arg -P plugin:org.jetbrains.kotlin.noarg:invokeInitializers=true. Maven users add <plugin>all-open</plugin> to the Kotlin Maven plugin with the kotlin-maven-allopen dependency. Since Kotlin 2.3.20, kotlin-maven-noarg also includes kotlin-maven-allopen.

kotlinx.serialization has more for data that changes over time. Open polymorphism, where subclasses live in other modules and the compiler can't see them all, needs a SerializersModule that registers each one. classDiscriminator renames the "type" field if your data already uses that name. coerceInputValues turns invalid values, such as an unknown enum constant, into the property's default instead of failing. And @JsonIgnoreUnknownKeys (Experimental) relaxes unknown keys for one class instead of a whole Json instance.

Finally, the generated code is plain JVM bytecode, fast and free of reflection while the program runs. That also makes it a good fit for native images, programs compiled ahead of time into a single executable, where reflection needs extra setup. The startup track covers why.
